claim: MHC class I proteins are cell surface proteins that control immune responses by CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells.
source: Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I proteins are cell surface proteins that control immune responses by CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about MHC class I function.

claim: MHC class I proteins are comprised of a heavy chain, a light chain (β2-microglobulin), and a short peptide bound to a peptide-binding groove in the heavy chain.
source: MHC class I proteins are comprised of a heavy chain, a light chain, β2-microglobulin (β2m), and a short peptide that is bound to a peptide-binding groove in the heavy chain (Bjorkman and Parham, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bjorkman and Parham, 1990.

claim: Heavy chains of human MHC molecules (HLA) are encoded by three sets of genes: HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C genes.
source: Heavy chains of human MHC molecules (human leukocyte antigens (HLA)) are encoded by three sets of genes, which are the HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HLA gene organization.

claim: HLA genes are highly polymorphic, with about 5000 known alleles in the case of HLA-B.
source: These genes are highly polymorphic, with about 5000 known alleles in the case of HLA-B and fewer alleles in the case of HLA-A and HLA-C genes (Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robinson et al., 2015.

claim: Polymorphic residues are localized to the peptide-binding groove of HLA class I proteins and determine their specificities for peptide binding.
source: Polymorphic residues are localized to the peptide-binding groove of HLA class I proteins and determine their specificities for peptide binding (Bjorkman and Parham, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bjorkman and Parham, 1990.

claim: T cell receptors (TCR) of cytotoxic T cells have specificities for combinations of MHC class I and peptide.
source: T cell receptors (TCR) of cytotoxic T cells have specificities for combinations of MHC class I and peptide (Rossjohn et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rossjohn et al., 2015.

claim: Binding of a CD8+ T cell TCR to peptide-MHC class I complexes triggers CD8+ T cell cytokine production and cytotoxic activity.
source: Binding of a CD8+ T cell TCR to peptide-MHC class I complexes triggers CD8+ T cell cytokine production and cytotoxic activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T cell activation.

claim: NK cells have inhibitory receptors that recognize HLA class I.
source: Conversely, NK cells have inhibitory receptors that recognize HLA class I (Saunders et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Saunders et al., 2015.

claim: Engagement of MHC class I by NK cell inhibitory receptors suppresses NK cell activity.
source: Engagement of MHC class I by NK cell inhibitory receptors suppresses NK cell activity (Parham and Moffett, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Parham and Moffett, 2013.

claim: NK cell activity is induced by MHC class I down-modulation, a strategy frequently used by viruses and cancers to evade CD8+ T cell responses.
source: NK cell activity is induced by MHC class I down-modulation, a strategy frequently used by viruses and cancers to evade CD8+ T cell responses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell activation and immune evasion strategies.

claim: MHC class I assembly involves a complex pathway that is initiated by the formation of chaperone-guided heterodimers of heavy chains and β2m.
source: MHC class I assembly involves a complex pathway that is initiated by the formation of chaperone-guided heterodimers of heavy chains and β2m.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC class I assembly.

claim: In the absence of a peptide ligand, heavy chain-β2m heterodimers are generally unstable and retained in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) via the peptide loading complex (PLC).
source: In the absence of a peptide ligand, heavy chain-β2m heterodimers are generally unstable and retained in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) via the peptide loading complex (PLC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC class I quality control.

claim: The PLC facilitates peptide loading of MHC class I, and comprises peptide-deficient forms of MHC class I molecules in complex with TAP, tapasin, calreticulin and ERp57.
source: The PLC facilitates peptide loading of MHC class I, and comprises peptide-deficient forms of MHC class I molecules in complex with the transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP), the assembly factor tapasin, and the ER chaperones calreticulin and ERp57.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PLC composition.

claim: The binding of a peptide releases MHC class I from the PLC, and allows for trafficking to the cell surface via the Golgi network.
source: The binding of a peptide releases MHC class I from the PLC, and allows for trafficking to the cell surface via the Golgi network (Blum et al., 2013; Raghavan and Geng, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blum et al., 2013 and Raghavan and Geng, 2015.

claim: HLA class I alleles have strong influences upon disease progression outcomes in infectious diseases and cancers.
source: HLA class I alleles have strong influences upon disease progression outcomes in infectious diseases and cancers (Carrington and Walker, 2012; Tang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carrington and Walker, 2012 and Tang et al., 2012.

claim: Specific HLA alleles are linked to autoimmune diseases.
source: Specific alleles are also linked to autoimmune diseases (Brown et al., 2016; Price et al., 1999) and drug hypersensitivities (Illing et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2016 and Price et al., 1999.

claim: Specific HLA alleles are linked to drug hypersensitivities.
source: Specific alleles are also linked to autoimmune diseases (Brown et al., 2016; Price et al., 1999) and drug hypersensitivities (Illing et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Illing et al., 2013.

claim: The peptide-binding characteristics of individual HLA class I molecules are important determinants of their associations with many disease outcomes.
source: Since the presence of a 'foreign' peptide is the key activation signal for CD8+ T cell responses, the peptide-binding characteristics of individual HLA class I molecules are important determinants of their associations with many disease outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of peptide-MHC complexes in T cell activation.

claim: The cell surface stabilities of HLA class I-peptide complexes can be influenced by multiple factors, including the nature of peptide-MHC interactions, the abundance of factors that mediate their assembly, and the extent of peptide-deficient HLA class I expression.
source: The cell surface stabilities of HLA class I-peptide complexes can be influenced by multiple factors, including the nature of peptide-MHC interactions, the abundance of factors that mediate their assembly, and the extent of peptide-deficient HLA class I expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on known factors affecting protein stability.

claim: A given HLA class I molecule can bind to a large number of peptides that have specific sequence motifs and length constraints.
source: A given HLA class I molecule can bind to a large number of peptides that have specific sequence motifs (for example, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and length constraints (the HLA class I peptidome, for example those characterized in [Abelin et al., 2017]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Abelin et al., 2017 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Not all HLA class I binding peptides are transported equivalently by the TAP transporter.
source: Not all HLA class I binding peptides are transported equivalently by the TAP transporter.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TAP peptide transport specificity.

claim: TAP has strong sequence preferences for peptide transport, with hydrophobic C-terminal residues preferred and proline at position 2 strongly disfavored.
source: The use of peptide libraries fixed at specific positions with single amino acids has revealed strong sequence preferences for peptide transport by TAP (Uebel et al., 1997). In general, peptide residue 2 (P2) and the C-terminal residues of peptides (PC) are strong determinants of peptide binding to HLA class I. TAP also has strong preferences within this region; hydrophobic C-terminal residues, generally preferred by HLA class I molecules, are also preferred by TAP. At the P2 position, however, proline is strongly disfavored by TAP, but highly preferred by a subset of HLA-B molecules - those within the B7 supertype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uebel et al., 1997 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Proline at position 2 is highly preferred by a subset of HLA-B molecules within the B7 supertype.
source: At the P2 position, however, proline is strongly disfavored by TAP, but highly preferred by a subset of HLA-B molecules - those within the B7 supertype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tapasin facilitates HLA class I-peptide assembly and optimizes the HLA class I peptide repertoire towards high affinity sequences.
source: A number of studies have indicated that tapasin, via the PLC, facilitates HLA class I-peptide assembly and also optimizes the HLA class I peptide repertoire towards high affinity sequences (Chen and Bouvier, 2007; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007; Williams et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen and Bouvier, 2007; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007; Williams et al., 2002.

claim: HLA-B allotypes differ markedly in their dependencies on tapasin for their cell surface expression.
source: HLA-B allotypes differ markedly in their dependencies on tapasin for their cell surface expression (Peh et al., 1998; Rizvi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peh et al., 1998 and Rizvi et al., 2014.

claim: Tapasin-independent HLA-B allotypes generally have higher intrinsic stabilities of their peptide-deficient forms.
source: Tapasin-independent HLA-B allotypes generally have higher intrinsic stabilities of their peptide-deficient forms (Rizvi et al., 2014), and thus may be more prone to exit the ER as suboptimally loaded versions, particularly when peptide is limiting.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rizvi et al., 2014.

claim: Tapasin-independent HLA-B allotypes may be more prone to exit the ER as suboptimally loaded versions, particularly when peptide is limiting.
source: Tapasin-independent HLA-B allotypes generally have higher intrinsic stabilities of their peptide-deficient forms (Rizvi et al., 2014), and thus may be more prone to exit the ER as suboptimally loaded versions, particularly when peptide is limiting.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the properties of tapasin-independent allotypes.

claim: mRNA differences and regulatory polymorphisms affect HLA class I and class II expression.
source: Previous studies have shown that mRNA differences and regulatory polymorphisms affect HLA class I and class II expression (Raj et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raj et al., 2016 and Thomas et al., 2009.

claim: The HLA-B locus is the most polymorphic of the HLA class I loci.
source: The HLA-B locus is the most polymorphic of the HLA class I loci (and thus the most rapidly evolving), with dominant influences upon disease outcomes (Kiepiela et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HLA-B polymorphism.

claim: The HLA-B locus has dominant influences upon disease outcomes.
source: The HLA-B locus is the most polymorphic of the HLA class I loci (and thus the most rapidly evolving), with dominant influences upon disease outcomes (Kiepiela et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kiepiela et al., 2004.

claim: HLA-B alleles do not vary in mRNA expression.
source: HLA-B alleles do not vary in mRNA expression (Ramsuran et al., 2017), but there are known variations in the assembly and peptide-binding characteristics of HLA-B allotypes, as described above.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ramsuran et al., 2017.

claim: The anti-Bw6 antibody was specific for HLA-B alleles with the Bw6 epitope, and showed no binding to any HLA-A or HLA-Bw4 allotypes.
source: The anti-Bw6 antibody was specific for HLA-B alleles with the Bw6 epitope, and showed no binding to any HLA-A or HLA-Bw4 allotypes, although it also recognized some HLA-C alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The anti-Bw6 antibody recognized some HLA-C alleles.
source: The anti-Bw6 antibody was specific for HLA-B alleles with the Bw6 epitope, and showed no binding to any HLA-A or HLA-Bw4 allotypes, although it also recognized some HLA-C alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: HLA-C alleles recognized by anti-Bw6 have a sequence motif similar to the Bw6 motif.
source: Further analyses of the sequences of the HLA-C alleles that were recognized by anti-Bw6 (residues 77–83) revealed the presence of a sequence motif similar to the Bw6 motif (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: HLA-B*08:01 has the highest expression measured among the tested HLA-Bw6 allotypes in lymphocytes.
source: In general, highest expression is measured for HLA-B*08:01 cells, and lowest expression is measured for HLA-B*07:02 and HLA-B*35:01 in all cell subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: HLA-B*07:02 and HLA-B*35:01 have the lowest expression measured among the tested HLA-Bw6 allotypes in lymphocytes.
source: In general, highest expression is measured for HLA-B*08:01 cells, and lowest expression is measured for HLA-B*07:02 and HLA-B*35:01 in all cell subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The expression differences between HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*07:02 are significant in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Based on a one-way ANOVA analysis, the expression differences between HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*07:02 are significant in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, but similar trends are noted in B and NK cell subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The expression differences between HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*35:01 are significant in CD4+, CD8+ T cells and NK cells.
source: Differences between HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*35:01 are significant in CD4+, CD8+ T cells and NK cells, but similar trends are noted in B cell subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 1.

claim: No significant differences between allele groups were measured in any cell type for the W6/32 ABC values.
source: On the other hand, no significant differences between allele groups were measured in any cell type for the W6/32 ABC values (Figure 1, column 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1, column 2.

claim: The Bw6/W6/32 ABC ratios were significantly higher for HLA-B*08:01 donors compared to B*07:02 donors in all cell types.
source: The Bw6/W6/32 ABC ratios were significantly higher for HLA-B*08:01 donors compared to B*07:02 donors in all cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The Bw6/W6/32 ABC ratios were significantly higher for HLA-B*08:01 donors compared to B*35:01 donors in CD4+, CD8+ T cells and NK cells.
source: Additionally, the Bw6/W6/32 ABC ratios were significantly higher for HLA-B*08:01 donors compared to B*35:01 donors in CD4+, CD8+ T cells and NK cells, and similar trends were noted in B cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Cell surface expression of HLA-B*07:02 and B*35:01 are low compared to other alleles, and significantly different compared to HLA-B*08:01.
source: Thus, based on the tested Bw6 group of alleles, cell surface expression of HLA-B*07:02 and B*35:01 are low compared to other alleles, and significantly different compared to HLA-B*08:01.
evidence: This is a summary of the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Both HLA-B*07:02 and HLA-B*35:01 prefer P2P peptides that are disfavored for TAP transport.
source: Notably, both these lowest expressing HLA-B allotypes prefer P2P peptides that are disfavored for TAP transport.
evidence: This is an inference based on the peptide-binding preferences of these allotypes and TAP transport specificity.

claim: HLA-B transcript levels are relatively invariant across alleles, based on measurements with PBMC.
source: Allele-dependent variations in RNA levels within cells can explain the surface expression differences (Figure 1), although recent findings indicate that HLA-B transcript levels are relatively invariant across alleles, based on measurments with PBMC (Ramsuran et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ramsuran et al., 2017.

claim: No significant differences are noted in HLA-B transcript levels using either HLA-B or pan HLA class I primers in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Based on a one-way ANOVA analysis, no significant differences are noted in transcript levels, using either HLA-B or pan HLA class I primers.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: There were no significant allele-dependent differences between HLA-B mRNA levels in CD4+ T cells, B cells and NK cells, based on samples derived from donors in Africa and Thailand.
source: There were no significant allele-dependent differences between HLA-B mRNA levels in CD4+ T cells, B cells and NK cells, based on samples derived from donors in Africa and Thailand.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The rate of assembly and exit from the ER for HLA-B*35:01 is so rapid that binding to peptide loading complex components in the ER is undetectable at the steady state in a CD4+ T cell line.
source: In a CD4+ T cell line, the rate of assembly and exit from the ER for HLA-B*35:01 is so rapid that binding to peptide loading complex components in the ER is undetectable at the steady state (Thammavongsa et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thammavongsa et al., 2009.

claim: It is unlikely that increased ER retention explains the lower surface expression of HLA-B*35:01.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that increased ER retention explains the lower surface expression of HLA-B*35:01.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid ER exit of HLA-B*35:01.

claim: The intracellular HLA-Bw6 protein levels are not higher in PBMCs from B*08:01 donors compared to cells from either HLA-B*35:01 or HLA-B*07:02 donors.
source: Consistent with this expectation, the intracellular HLA-Bw6 protein levels (quantified as a ratio of the fluorescence signal in fixed relative to fixed and permeabilized cells (fixed/fixed +permeabilized) in flow cytometry experiments are not higher in PBMCs from B*08:01 donors compared to cells from either HLA-B*35:01 or HLA-B*07:02 donors (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished data.

claim: HLA-B*08:01 displays high cell surface stability compared to all other HLA-Bw6 allotypes in lymphocytes.
source: HLA-B*08:01, in general, displays high cell surface stability compared to all other HLA-Bw6 allotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by half-life data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The most significant half-life differences are between HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*35:01 in lymphocytes.
source: Based on a one-way ANOVA analysis, the most significant differences are between HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*35:01 - allotypes which display the most significant cell surface expression differences (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of half-life data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The half-life differences between HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*35:01 are most significant in CD8+ T cells.
source: The differences are most significant in CD8+ T cells, although significant trends are also noted in CD4+ T cells and NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of half-life data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The half-life differences between HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*35:01 are significant in all cells based on pairwise comparisons.
source: In pairwise comparisons based on a Welch's t-test (not shown), the half-life differences between HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*35:01 are significant in all cells, and those between HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*07:02 are significant in all cells except B cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of half-life data.

claim: The high steady state cell-surface expression levels of HLA-B*08:01 relative to HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 in lymphocytes can be explained by the higher cell surface stability of HLA-B*08:01.
source: Overall, the half-life measurements indicate that the high steady state cell-surface expression levels of HLA-B*08:01 relative to HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-B*07:02 in lymphocytes can be explained by the higher cell surface stability of HLA-B*08:01.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between expression levels and half-lives.

claim: Expression differences between B*08:01 and B*07:02/B*35:01 were significant in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in monocyte measurements.
source: Expression differences between B*08:01 and B*07:02/B*35:01 were significant in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 3A), consistent with the previous measurements with the larger pool of donors (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For monocyte measurements, the expression differences were reversed, with B*08:01 displaying lower expression than both B*35:01 and B*07:02.
source: Surprisingly, however, for the parallel monocyte measurements within the same pool of donors, the expression differences were reversed, with B*08:01 displaying lower expression than both B*35:01 and B*07:02, and the differences reaching statistical significance for B*35:01 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Monocytes displayed a significant induction of expression relative to CD4+ and CD8+ T cells for B*35:01 and B*07:02, but not for B*08:01.
source: When the monocyte ABC values for each donor were normalized relative to their CD4+ and CD8+ T cell ABC values and donors grouped by their Bw6 alleles, monocytes displayed a significant induction of expression relative to CD4+ and CD8+ T cells for B*35:01 and B*07:02, but not for B*08:01 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a significant reduction in B*08:01 half-life in monocytes compared with CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Corresponding half-life measurements indicated a significant reduction in B*08:01 half-life in monocytes compared with CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, whereas the differences between monocytes and lymphocytes were not significant for B*07:02 and B*35:01 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In monocytes, no significant half-life differences were measured between B*08:01 and B*35:01/B*07:02.
source: Indeed, in monocytes, no significant half-life differences were measured between B*08:01 and B*35:01/B*07:02 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There are both allele and cell type dependent variations in HLA-B cell surface expression and stability patterns.
source: Together, these findings indicated both allele and cell type dependent variations in HLA-B cell surface expression and stability patterns.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figures 1-3.

claim: Monocytes have more intracellular HLA class I relative to lymphocyte populations.
source: Based on these experiments, monocytes were found to have more intracellular HLA class I relative to lymphocytes populations (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Monocytes have higher expression of TAP1 and higher activity of TAP complexes relative to lymphocytes.
source: Previous studies have described higher expression of TAP1 and higher activity of TAP complexes in monocytes relative to lymphocytes (Fischbach et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fischbach et al., 2015.

claim: Monocytes generally have more tapasin relative to lymphocytes.
source: Additionally, monocytes generally also have more tapasin relative to lymphocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tapasin/W6/32 ratios are lower in monocytes compared with lymphocytes.
source: However, the tapasin/W6/32 ratios are lower in monocytes compared with lymphocytes (Figure 4B), suggesting that tapasin is more limiting in monocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Tapasin is more limiting in monocytes compared with lymphocytes.
source: However, the tapasin/W6/32 ratios are lower in monocytes compared with lymphocytes (Figure 4B), suggesting that tapasin is more limiting in monocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lower tapasin/W6/32 ratios in monocytes.

claim: The lower tapasin/W6/32 ratios in monocytes could at least in part explain the reduced half-life in monocytes compared with lymphocytes for HLA-B*08:01, a strongly tapasin-dependent allotype.
source: These differences could at least in part explain the reduced half-life in monocytes compared with lymphocytes for HLA-B*08:01, a strongly tapasin-dependent allotype (Rizvi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the tapasin-dependence of HLA-B*08:01 and the lower tapasin/W6/32 ratios in monocytes.

claim: There is significantly greater co-localization between intracellular HLA-Bw6 and AP-1, compared with co-localization between HLA-Bw6 and either calreticulin or LAMP-1 in both monocytes and T lymphocytes.
source: The imaging cytometry quantifications indicated significantly greater co-localization between intracellular HLA-Bw6 and AP-1, compared with co-localization between HLA-Bw6 and either calreticulin or LAMP-1. The greater HLA-Bw6 and AP-1 co-localization is measured in both monocytes and T lymphocytes (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging cytometry data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: There were no strong differences in Bw6/AP-1 co-localization between cells from a B*08:01 donor and a B*07:02 donor.
source: Additionally, there were no strong differences in Bw6/AP-1 co-localization between cells from a B*08:01 donor and a B*07:02 donor, suggesting that B7 supertype members do not co-localize or interact differently with AP-1 than B*08:01 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging cytometry data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: B7 supertype members do not co-localize or interact differently with AP-1 than B*08:01.
source: Additionally, there were no strong differences in Bw6/AP-1 co-localization between cells from a B*08:01 donor and a B*07:02 donor, suggesting that B7 supertype members do not co-localize or interact differently with AP-1 than B*08:01 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of differences in Bw6/AP-1 co-localization between B*08:01 and B*07:02.

claim: Both B*08:01 and B*07:02 allotypes exit the ER, as evidenced by the lower proportion of cells with high Bw6/calreticulin co-localization.
source: Despite the reduced tapasin/HLA class I ratios in monocytes relative to lymphocytes (Figure 4B), both B*08:01 and B*07:02 allotypes exit the ER, as evidenced by the lower proportion of cells with high Bw6/calreticulin co-localization (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the low Bw6/calreticulin co-localization shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The AP-1+ compartment could provide a source of peptides that accounts for the strong cell surface induction of HLA-B*07:02 and HLA-B*35:01 in monocytes compared with lymphocytes.
source: The AP-1+ compartment could provide a source of peptides that accounts for the strong cell surface induction of HLA-B*07:02 and HLA-B*35:01 in monocytes compared with lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the presence of HLA-B in the AP-1+ compartment and the expression patterns in monocytes.

claim: In lymphocytes, HLA class I trafficking differences result in a smaller intracellular pool of HLA class I.
source: On the other hand, in lymphocytes, HLA class I trafficking differences result in a smaller intracellular pool of HLA class I (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The smaller pool of intracellular class I in lymphocytes could render the HLA class I of lymphocytes more reliant on a TAP-dependent ER pool of peptides.
source: The smaller pool of the intracellular class I could render the HLA class I of lymphocytes more reliant on a TAP-dependent ER pool of peptides.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the smaller intracellular pool of HLA class I in lymphocytes.

claim: Mismatches between the peptide binding preferences of HLA-B7 supertype members and TAP may be more strongly manifested in lymphocytes.
source: As a consequence, mismatches between the peptide binding preferences of HLA-B7 supertype members and TAP may be more strongly manifested in lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the reliance of lymphocytes on TAP-dependent peptides.

claim: There is overall greater receptivity of HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 for peptides compared with HLA-B*08:01 in B cells and CD4+ T cells.
source: Analyses of the HC10 ratio (specific/control peptide; Figure 5) indicate that there is in fact overall greater receptivity of HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 for peptides compared with HLA-B*08:01 in B cells and CD4+ T cells with similar trends observed in NK cells and CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by HC10 staining data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Peptide loading of HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 does not require internalization, and cell surface HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 are at least partially directly peptide-receptive.
source: Assessment of the temperature dependence of surface peptide loading suggests that peptide loading does not require internalization, and thus that cell surface HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 are at least partially directly peptide-receptive (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished data on temperature dependence of peptide loading.

claim: The high peptide receptivity of HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 and low surface expression in lymphocytes are consistent with the model that the intracellular peptide pool for those allotypes is limiting owing to their P2P binding preferences.
source: In lymphocytes, the high peptide receptivity of HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 and low surface expression are consistent with the model that the intracellular peptide pool for those allotypes is limiting owing to their P2P binding preferences, which is disfavored for transport by TAP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the peptide receptivity and expression data.

claim: HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 have high or intermediate tapasin-independence for their assembly.
source: HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 have high or intermediate tapasin-independence for their assembly, and thus it is likely that sub-optimally assembled or peptide-deficient versions of these allotypes can escape quality control mechanisms mediated by the PLC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tapasin-dependence of these allotypes.

claim: Sub-optimally assembled or peptide-deficient versions of HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 can escape quality control mechanisms mediated by the PLC.
source: HLA-B*35:01 and HLA-B*07:02 have high or intermediate tapasin-independence for their assembly, and thus it is likely that sub-optimally assembled or peptide-deficient versions of these allotypes can escape quality control mechanisms mediated by the PLC.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the tapasin-independence of these allotypes.

claim: Monocyte HLA-B are not receptive to exogenous peptides for HLA-B*08:01, B*35:01, or for B*07:02.
source: On the other hand, monocyte HLA-B are not receptive to exogenous peptides for HLA-B*08:01, B*35:01, or for B*07:02.
evidence: This claim is supported by HC10 staining data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The reduced stability of HLA-B*08:01 in monocytes relative to lymphocytes is not accompanied by enhanced cell surface peptide receptivity in monocytes.
source: The reduced stability of HLA-B*08:01 (Figure 3D) in monocytes relative to lymphocytes is not accompanied by enhanced cell surface peptide receptivity in monocytes (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3D and 5.

claim: The findings are consistent with the overall model of suboptimal assembly of B*35:01 and B*07:02 in lymphocytes.
source: Taken together, the findings are consistent with the overall model of suboptimal assembly of B*35:01 and B*07:02 in lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the peptide receptivity and expression data.

claim: Lymphocytes and monocytes maintain their cell surface HLA-B via different mechanisms, which in turn differently influence their exogenous peptide-receptivity.
source: Furthermore, the results indicate that lymphocytes and monocytes maintain their cell surface HLA-B via different mechanisms, which in turn differently influence their exogenous peptide-receptivity.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the differences in expression, stability, and peptide receptivity between lymphocytes and monocytes.

claim: The anti-Bw4 antibody is specific for HLA-B alleles within the HLA-Bw4 group and does not bind HLA-Bw6 alleles or HLA-C alleles.
source: For these measurements, the anti-Bw4 antibody from One Lambda was used, which is specific for HLA-B alleles within the HLA-Bw4 group and does not bind HLA-Bw6 alleles or HLA-C alleles. However, five HLA-A alleles are recognized (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; A*23:01, A*24:02, A*24:03, A*25:01, A*32:01).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Five HLA-A alleles are recognized by the anti-Bw4 antibody (A*23:01, A*24:02, A*24:03, A*25:01, A*32:01).
source: However, five HLA-A alleles are recognized (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; A*23:01, A*24:02, A*24:03, A*25:01, A*32:01).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HLA-A alleles recognized by anti-Bw4 have a sequence motif similar to the Bw4 motif.
source: Further analyses of the sequences of the HLA-A alleles that are recognized by anti-Bw4 (residues 77–83) revealed the presence of a sequence motif similar to the Bw4 motif (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The anti-Bw4 antibody showed considerable binding variability within the selected group of HLA-Bw4 alleles.
source: Within this selected group of HLA-Bw4 alleles, the anti-Bw4 antibody showed considerable binding variability (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant differences in HLA-Bw4 ABC values are measured in all four cell types based on a one-way ANOVA analysis.
source: Significant differences in HLA-Bw4 ABC values are measured in all four cell types based on a one-way ANOVA analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Many cell subsets showed significant differences between B*57:01/B*27:05 and other HLA-Bw4 allotypes.
source: Many cell subsets showed significant differences between B*57:01/B*27:05 and other HLA-Bw4 allotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The Luminex binding analyses indicated the highest binding preference of anti-Bw4 for HLA-B*57:01 and HLA-B*27:05.
source: This is similar to the pattern seen with the Luminex binding analyses, which indicated the highest binding preference of anti-Bw4 for HLA-B*57:01 and HLA-B*27:05 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A correlation analysis of the Luminex bead Bw4/W6/32 ratio versus cell-derived Bw4 ABC values showed significant positive correlations in all lymphocytes.
source: A correlation analysis of the Luminex bead Bw4/W6/32 ratio versus cell-derived Bw4 ABC values showed significant positive correlations in all lymphocytes (Figure 6, column 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6, column 1.

claim: The varying anti-Bw4 binding preferences contribute to differences in the observed cell-derived Bw4 ABC values.
source: These analyses indicated that the varying anti-Bw4 binding preferences contribute to differences in the observed cell-derived Bw4 ABC values.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between Luminex binding and cell-derived ABC values.

claim: The averaged HLA-B*51:01 ABC value on cells is lower than that expected based on the measured anti-Bw4 binding preferences.
source: However, whereas in the Luminex bead analyses, the binding preference was HLA-B*57:01 > HLA-B*27:05 > HLA-B*51:01 > HLA-B*37:01 = HLA-B*13:02 > HLA-B*44:02 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), the general Bw4 ABC value trends (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, column 1) indicated that the averaged HLA-B*51:01 ABC value on cells is lower than that expected based on the measured anti-Bw4 binding preferences, and resemble the B*44:02 signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The majority of HLA-B*51:01 ABC values fall below the linear regression line of the correlation plot in all the tested cells.
source: Correspondingly, the majority of HLA-B*51:01 ABC values fall below the linear regression line of the correlation plot in all the tested cells (Figure 6, column 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6, column 1.

claim: No significant half-life differences were measurable for HLA-B*51:01 compared to other HLA-Bw4 alleles in any of the cell types.
source: No significant half-life differences were measurable for HLA-B*51:01 compared to other HLA-Bw4 alleles in any of the cell types (Figure 6, column 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by half-life data shown in Figure 6, column 3.

claim: A limiting supply of peptides may create an intracellular assembly bottleneck for B*51:01.
source: A limiting supply of peptides may create an intracellular assembly bottleneck for B*51:01 (which is highly tapasin-dependent; [Rizvi et al., 2014]), which requires further assessments.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the tapasin-dependence of B*51:01 and its P2P binding preference.

claim: The lowest expressing Bw4 allele in lymphocytes is a member of the B7 supertype, and has a P2P peptide-binding preference that is disfavored for TAP transport.
source: Overall, as with Bw6 alleles, the lowest expressing Bw4 allele in lymphocytes is a member of the B7 supertype, and has a P2P peptide-binding preference that is disfavored for TAP transport.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings for Bw4 alleles.

claim: The averaged B*51:01 ABC values are lower than those for B*57:01, and comparable to B*44:02 in B cells.
source: The averaged B*51:01 ABC values are lower than those for B*57:01, and comparable to B*44:02 in B cells, as previously noted with the larger pool of donors (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, column 1), although differences become non-significant with the smaller pool of donors in Figure 7A.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: In monocytes, B*51:01 becomes strongly induced compared with lymphocytes, whereas there is a small change for B*57:01, and a reduction for B*44:02.
source: Again, surprisingly, these expression trends become altered in monocytes, where B*51:01 becomes strongly induced compared with lymphocytes, whereas there is a small change for B*57:01, and a reduction for B*44:02 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The expression patterns obtained with W6/32 in monocytes mirrored those obtained with anti-Bw4.
source: It is noteworthy that the expression patterns obtained with W6/32 in monocytes mirrored those obtained with anti-Bw4 (Figure 7B), indicating that variations in single HLA-B allele expression levels significantly impact total HLA class I levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Variations in single HLA-B allele expression levels significantly impact total HLA class I levels.
source: It is noteworthy that the expression patterns obtained with W6/32 in monocytes mirrored those obtained with anti-Bw4 (Figure 7B), indicating that variations in single HLA-B allele expression levels significantly impact total HLA class I levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of W6/32 and anti-Bw4 expression patterns.

claim: Significant increases and decreases in expression were measured respectively for B*51:01 and B*4402 in monocytes compared with lymphocytes.
source: When the ABC values for B cells were normalized relative to the monocyte values for each donor, significant increases and decreases in expression were measured respectively for B*51:01 and B*4402 in monocytes compared with lymphocytes (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: With the reduction in the number of alleles examined, a significant correlation was obtained in monocytes that have the high B*51:01 expression, but not in lymphocytes.
source: With the reduction in the number of alleles examined, a significant correlation was obtained in monocytes that have the high B*51:01 expression, but not in lymphocytes, where B*51:01 expression is lower than predicted by the Luminex bead binding (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The cellular assembly landscape of monocytes favors B*51:01 cell surface expression and disfavors B*44:02 expression, whereas cell surface expression of B*51:01 is disfavored in lymphocytes.
source: Thus, the cellular assembly landscape of monocytes favors B*51:01 cell surface expression and disfavors B*44:02 expression, whereas cell surface expression of B*51:01 is disfavored in lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the expression patterns in monocytes and lymphocytes.

claim: B*08:01 is unusual for its unique P5 anchor, resembling the anchor residue positioning in murine MHC class I molecules.
source: B*08:01 is unusual not only for its unique P5 anchor (resembling the anchor residue positioning in murine MHC class I molecules), but also in having restrictive P3 and Pc-1 residues in addition to the restrictions at P2 and Pc (Figure 8 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Shannon entropy plots shown in Figure 8 and peptide motifs in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: B*08:01 has restrictive P3 and Pc-1 residues in addition to the restrictions at P2 and Pc.
source: B*08:01 is unusual not only for its unique P5 anchor (resembling the anchor residue positioning in murine MHC class I molecules), but also in having restrictive P3 and Pc-1 residues in addition to the restrictions at P2 and Pc (Figure 8 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Shannon entropy plots shown in Figure 8 and peptide motifs in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In B*08:01, the overall geometry is different from other HLA-B allotypes including HLA-B*35:01.
source: In B*08:01, the overall geometry is different from other HLA-B allotypes including HLA-B*35:01.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: E45 and F67 of HLA-B*08:01 move away from the P2 pocket and F36 spatially substitutes for E45.
source: In B*08:01, the overall geometry is different from other HLA-B allotypes including HLA-B*35:01. E45 and F67 of HLA-B*08:01 move away from the P2 pocket and F36 spatially substitutes for E45.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: B*08:01 has ionic interactions between D9 and a deeply buried peptide residue at P5.
source: In addition to the non-polar interaction of residues P2 and PC of the peptide with non-polar clusters of protein residues (P2 with F36 and PC with L81-L95-Y116-Y123), B*08:01 has ionic interactions between D9 and a deeply buried peptide residue at P5.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Comparisons of crystal structures of HLA class I peptide complexes have revealed fully extended and deeply buried peptides for HLA-B*08:01 compared to other HLA-B allotypes, including HLA-B*35:01 and B*07:02.
source: Indeed, as a result of these multiple contact points, comparisons of crystal structures of HLA class I peptide complexes have revealed fully extended and deeply buried peptides for HLA-B*08:01 compared to other HLA-B allotypes, including HLA-B*35:01 and B*07:02 (Maenaka et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maenaka et al., 2000.

claim: The unique peptide-binding characteristics of HLA-B*08:01 are likely to underlie its high cell surface stability in lymphocytes.
source: These unique peptide-binding characteristics of HLA-B*08:01 are likely to underlie its high cell surface stability in lymphocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural features of HLA-B*08:01 and its high stability.

claim: HLA-B alleles do not vary in their mRNA expression in individual lymphocyte subsets.
source: HLA-B alleles do not vary in their mRNA expression in individual lymphocyte subsets, as previously described in bulk PBMC (Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5 and (Ramsuran et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5, and a citation to Ramsuran et al., 2017.

claim: Both allele-intrinsic and cell-intrinsic factors exert important influences on HLA-B cell surface protein expressions levels.
source: However, both allele-intrinsic and cell-intrinsic factors exert important influences on HLA-B cell surface protein expressions levels.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: There is no global high or low cell surface expressing allotype among the 12 HLA-B alleles considered in this study; rather, measured variations are cell-specific.
source: Nonetheless, there is no global high or low cell surface expressing allotype among the 12 HLA-B alleles considered in this study; rather, measured variations are cell-specific (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings shown in Figure 9.

claim: There are allele and cell type-dependent thresholds for passing ER quality control checkpoints rather than a global threshold for HLA class I stability.
source: Furthermore, there are allele and cell type-dependent thresholds for passing ER quality control checkpoints rather than a global threshold for HLA class I stability.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: Mismatch of HLA peptide binding preference with TAP transport specificity (P2P preferences of the B7 superfamily) is a potential determinant of low cell surface expression in lymphocytes.
source: Mismatch of HLA peptide binding preference with TAP transport specificity (P2P preferences of the B7 superfamily) is a potential determinant of low cell surface expression in lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: A tapasin-independent assembly pathway is a potential factor for reduced cell surface expression and stability and enhanced exogenous peptide-receptivity in lymphocytes, particularly when the intracellular peptide pool is also limiting.
source: A tapasin-independent assembly pathway is also a potential factor for reduced cell surface expression and stability and enhanced exogenous peptide-receptivity in lymphocytes, particularly when the intracellular peptide pool is also limiting.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: High affinity peptides are better able to displace tapasin from HLA class I than low affinity peptides.
source: High affinity peptides are better able to displace tapasin from HLA class I than low affinity peptides (Rizvi and Raghavan, 2006), consistent with recent structural studies (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017) that support models involving competition between peptide and tapasin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rizvi and Raghavan, 2006; Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017.

claim: For MHC class I allotypes assembling in the context of the PLC, the threshold peptide affinity required to exit the ER is expected to be dictated by the affinity of the tapasin-MHC interaction.
source: For MHC class I allotypes assembling in the context of the PLC, the threshold peptide affinity required to exit the ER is expected to be dictated by the affinity of the tapasin-MHC interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of tapasin in peptide loading.

claim: For allotypes such as HLA-B*35:01 and B*07:02 that can assemble efficiently independently of the PLC, the threshold affinity for ER exit would be lower than allotypes such as B*08:01, which are more dependent on the PLC for assembly.
source: For allotypes such as HLA-B*35:01 and B*07:02 that can also assemble efficiently independently of the PLC, this threshold affinity would be lower than allotypes such as B*08:01, which are more dependent on the PLC for assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tapasin-dependence of different allotypes.

claim: Allotypes such as HLA-B*35:01 and B*07:02 may escape PLC-mediated and other ER quality control mechanisms when devoid of peptides or when bound to a sub-optimal peptide, resulting in enhanced peptide receptivity in lymphocytes.
source: Since tapasin-independent assembly is also linked to higher stability of the peptide-deficient form (Rizvi et al., 2014), allotypes such as HLA-B*35:01 and B*07:02 may escape PLC-mediated and other ER quality control mechanisms when devoid of peptides or when bound to a sub-optimal peptide, resulting in enhanced peptide receptivity in lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the tapasin-independence and stability of these allotypes.

claim: Tapasin-dependent allotypes such as B*51:01 that have P2P preferences may face an intracellular assembly bottleneck.
source: Alternatively, tapasin-dependent allotypes such as B*51:01 that have P2P preferences may face an intracellular assembly bottleneck.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the tapasin-dependence and P2P preference of B*51:01.

claim: High expression and stability of B*08:01 in lymphocytes is linked to its unique peptide-binding characteristics, an ample peptide supply and tapasin-dependent assembly.
source: Conversely, high expression and stability of B*08:01 in lymphocytes is linked to its unique peptide-binding characteristics (Figure 8), an ample peptide supply and tapasin-dependent assembly.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: In monocytes, an intracellular AP-1+ compartment contains a large pool of intracellular HLA-B, and assembly parameters within this compartment are likely to account for monocyte-specific HLA-B cell surface expression differences.
source: With regard to cell-intrinsic factors, in monocytes, an intracellular AP-1+ compartment contains a large pool of intracellular HLA-B, and assembly parameters within this compartment are likely to account for monocyte-specific HLA-B cell surface expression differences (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings shown in Figure 4.

claim: A more substantial pool of HLA-B is intracellularly localized in monocytes than lymphocytes.
source: While further studies are needed to understand the differences between HLA-B assembly in monocytes and lymphocytes, it is apparent that a more substantial pool of HLA-B is intracellularly localized in monocytes than lymphocytes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Peptides that enter the intracellular compartments independently of TAP may provide a robust peptide source for members of the B7 supertype in monocytes.
source: Peptides that enter the intracellular compartments independently of TAP may provide a robust peptide source for members of the B7 supertype in monocytes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the presence of HLA-B in the AP-1+ compartment.

claim: HLA-B allotypes with P2P preferences generally tend to express at higher levels under TAP-deficiency conditions.
source: Indeed, in a related study (Geng et al., 2018), we find that HLA-B allotypes with P2P preferences generally tend to express at higher levels under TAP-deficiency conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Geng et al., 2018.

claim: The reduced tapasin/HLA class I ratios in monocytes are likely to induce greater competition for the formation of stoichiometric tapasin:HLA class I complexes within the PLC.
source: Furthermore, despite the presence of higher levels of tapasin in monocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the parallel increases in HLA class I levels (and reduced tapasin/HLA class I ratios; (Figure 4B)) are likely to induce greater competition for the formation of stoichiometric tapasin:HLA class I complexes within the PLC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tapasin/HLA class I ratios shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Competition for tapasin, combined with the particular environment within the AP-1+ compartment, could selectively reduce the assembly efficiency and/or the assembly quality of allotypes such as HLA-B*44:02 and B*08:01 in monocytes.
source: Such competition, combined with the particular environment within the AP-1+ compartment, could selectively reduce the assembly efficiency and/or the assembly quality of allotypes such as HLA-B*44:02 and B*08:01 in monocytes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the reduced tapasin/HLA class I ratios and the AP-1+ compartment.

claim: The measurements with lymphocytes and monocytes highlight the importance of the cellular assembly landscape as a key HLA-B cell surface expression determinant.
source: Overall, the measurements with lymphocytes and monocytes highlight the importance of the cellular assembly landscape as a key HLA-B cell surface expression determinant (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: A recent study reported higher expression of HLA-B*57 and HLA-B*27 relative to other Bw4 allotypes including HLA-B*44 in bulk PBMCs.
source: A recent study reported higher expression of HLA-B*57 and HLA-B*27 relative to other Bw4 allotypes including HLA-B*44 in bulk PBMCs (Boudreau et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Boudreau et al., 2016.

claim: The results of Boudreau et al., 2016 can be explained by variations in recognition by the anti-Bw4 antibody that was used.
source: Those results can be explained by variations in recognition by the anti-Bw4 antibody that was used, which was the same antibody used as in our Bw4 measurements (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the antibody binding data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 4.

claim: A study found low cell surface expression among some chicken MHC allotypes, which was attributed to their promiscuous binding of peptides lacking recognizable anchor residues.
source: Another recent study found low cell surface expression among some chicken MHC allotypes, which was attributed to their promiscuous binding of peptides lacking recognizable anchor residues (Chappell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chappell et al., 2015.

claim: A study reported high expression of cell surface HLA-B in lymphocytes and monocytes of homozygous donors expressing HLA-B*27:05 and HLA-B*57:01 compared with donors expressing B*07:02 and B*35:01.
source: Using a different set of antibodies than anti-Bw4/Bw6, the study also reported high expression of cell surface HLA-B in lymphocytes and monocytes of homozygous donors expressing HLA-B*27:05 and HLA-B*57:01 compared with donors expressing B*07:02 and B*35:01.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chappell et al., 2015.

claim: Higher promiscuity of the B*07:02 and B*35:01 peptidomes relative to those of B*27:05 and HLA-B*57:01 was suggested based on prior studies.
source: Higher promiscuity of the B*07:02 and B*35:01 peptidomes relative to those of B*27:05 and HLA-B*57:01 was suggested based on prior studies (Chappell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chappell et al., 2015.

claim: Shannon Entropy plots of mass spectrometry-derived 9-mer peptides suggest higher P2 diversity for B*57:01 compared to B*35:01.
source: While it is likely that mass spectrometry does not capture the full peptidome diversity, Shannon Entropy plots of mass spectrometry-derived 9-mer peptides suggest higher P2 diversity for B*57:01 compared to B*35:01, confirmed by motif assessments with a different peptidome dataset (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Assessments of length diversities indicate similar preferences of B*57:01 compared to B*35:01 for 9-mer and 10-mer peptides relative to other lengths.
source: Assessments of length diversities indicate similar preferences of B*57:01 compared to B*35:01 for 9-mer and 10-mer peptides relative to other lengths (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished data.

claim: There is not a simple relationship between HLA-B expression levels and peptidome diversity.
source: Overall, our findings suggest that there is a not a simple relationship between HLA-B expression levels and peptidome diversity, and indeed that intracellular assembly variations can induce different peptidome diversities for the same allotype in different cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: Intracellular assembly variations can induce different peptidome diversities for the same allotype in different cells.
source: Overall, our findings suggest that there is a not a simple relationship between HLA-B expression levels and peptidome diversity, and indeed that intracellular assembly variations can induce different peptidome diversities for the same allotype in different cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: The HLA 8.1 ancestral haplotype, which includes the HLA-B*08:01 allele, has been associated with a number of autoimmune diseases.
source: The HLA 8.1 ancestral haplotype, which includes the HLA-B*08:01 allele, has been associated with a number of autoimmune diseases (Candore et al., 2002; Price et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Candore et al., 2002 and Price et al., 1999.

claim: Genetic studies show that the strongest individual allelic associations for polymyositis are with HLA-B*08:01.
source: Recent genetic studies show that the strongest individual allelic associations for polymyositis are with HLA-B*08:01 (Miller et al., 2015) and another study showed strong HLA-B*08:01 associations with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (Rothwell et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2015 and Rothwell et al., 2016.

claim: High cell-surface expression and high cell-surface stability of HLA-B*08:01 in lymphocytes may lead to increased probability of CD8+ T cell activation in autoimmune myopathies.
source: Our findings indicate high cell-surface expression and high cell-surface stability of HLA-B*08:01 in lymphocytes, relating to the specifics of peptide interactions with HLA-B*08:01 (Figure 8), which may lead to increased probability of CD8+ T cell activation in autoimmune myopathies.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the high expression and stability of HLA-B*08:01.

claim: Conditional upregulation of HLA class I in muscle is sufficient to induce some characteristics of autoimmune myositis in mouse models of disease.
source: Conditional upregulation of HLA class I in muscle is sufficient to induce some characteristics of autoimmune myositis in mouse models of disease (Nagaraju et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nagaraju et al., 2000.

claim: The influences of HLA class I expression levels on the lysis of HIV-infected CD4+ T cells by cytotoxic CD8+ T cells is well-studied.
source: The influences of HLA class I expression levels on the lysis of HIV-infected CD4+ T cells by cytotoxic CD8+ T cells is well-studied (Collins et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Collins et al., 1998.

claim: HLA-B alleles have strong influences on AIDS progression outcomes and viral loads.
source: HLA-B alleles have strong influences on AIDS progression outcomes and viral loads (Bashirova et al., 2014; Carrington and Walker, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bashirova et al., 2014 and Carrington and Walker, 2012.

claim: High HLA-B expression in APC lineage cells would favor effective priming of an HIV-specific CD8+ T cell response and their activity against infected macrophages.
source: High HLA-B expression in APC lineage cells would favor effective priming of an HIV-specific CD8+ T cell response and their activity against infected macrophages, whereas high HLA-B expression in CD4+ T cells would favor efficient CD8+ T cell-mediated lysis of infected CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the role of HLA-B in T cell responses.

claim: High HLA-B expression in CD4+ T cells would favor efficient CD8+ T cell-mediated lysis of infected CD4+ T cells.
source: High HLA-B expression in APC lineage cells would favor effective priming of an HIV-specific CD8+ T cell response and their activity against infected macrophages, whereas high HLA-B expression in CD4+ T cells would favor efficient CD8+ T cell-mediated lysis of infected CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the role of HLA-B in T cell responses.

claim: The B*57:01 advantage in HIV infections relative to less protective HLA-Bw4 allotypes such as B*51:01 and B*44:02 may derive in part from the relatively high expression of B*57:01 in both cell lineages.
source: The B*57:01 advantage in HIV infections relative to less protective HLA-Bw4 allotypes such as B*51:01 and B*44:02 may derive in part from the relatively high expression of B*57:01 in both cell lineages.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the expression patterns of B*57:01.

claim: The B*35:01 disadvantage in HIV infections may relate in part to its lower expression, lower stability and higher proportion of peptide-deficient versions in CD4+ T cells.
source: Similarly, the B*35:01 disadvantage may relate in part to its lower expression, lower stability and higher proportion of peptide-deficient versions in CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the expression and stability patterns of B*35:01.

claim: Quality control mediated by peptide loading complex (PLC) components is expected to ensure the cell surface expression of stable peptide-HLA class I complexes.
source: Quality control mediated by peptide loading complex (PLC) components is expected to ensure the cell surface expression of stable peptide-HLA class I complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PLC function.

claim: HLA-B*08:01 in primary human lymphocytes has both expression level and half-life at the high end of the measured HLA-B expression and stability hierarchies.
source: This is exemplified by HLA-B*08:01 in primary human lymphocytes, with both expression level and half-life at the high end of the measured HLA-B expression and stability hierarchies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Low expression on lymphocytes is measured for three HLA-B allotypes that bind peptides with proline at position 2, which are disfavored by the transporter associated with antigen processing.
source: Conversely, low expression on lymphocytes is measured for three HLA-B allotypes that bind peptides with proline at position 2, which are disfavored by the transporter associated with antigen processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Lymphocyte-specific expression and stability differences become reversed or altered in monocytes.
source: Surprisingly, these lymphocyte-specific expression and stability differences become reversed or altered in monocytes, which display larger intracellular pools of HLA class I than lymphocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Monocytes display larger intracellular pools of HLA class I than lymphocytes.
source: Surprisingly, these lymphocyte-specific expression and stability differences become reversed or altered in monocytes, which display larger intracellular pools of HLA class I than lymphocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Allele and cell-dependent variations in antigen acquisition pathways influence HLA-B surface expression levels, half-lives and receptivity to exogenous antigens.
source: Together, the findings indicate that allele and cell-dependent variations in antigen acquisition pathways influence HLA-B surface expression levels, half-lives and receptivity to exogenous antigens.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.
